name: Tamang
confidence_why: Hari, Taylor and Pike (1970), working on the Nuwakot dialect, state that word stress always falls on the first syllable, but Mazaudon (2005), the principal Tamang specialist whose own fieldwork is on Eastern Tamang, remarks in passing that Tamang syllables appear about equally stressed, and Regmi (2019) says only that stress is not distinctive, so the initial-stress reading rests on one older first-hand description that no later study confirms or directly refutes.

sweep_summary: Only one titled item for west2415: Pittman 1970 'Gurung, Tamang, Thakali, Sherpa, and Chepang prosodies' (Part II of the Hale & Pike SIL report, ERIC ED046002). The full Part II scan (24 MB, 136 pp.) was downloaded from archive.org and the Pittman paper read in full (the scanned text): it is a comparative register/tone paper in which Tamang 'high/mid/low stressed vs unstressed' are four lexical word-base classes matched to Gurung/Thakali tone classes; it makes no statement about which syllable carries stress, so it is silent on the catalog's classification (fixed: initial syllable), and Part I's editors state Hari's later analysis supersedes this scheme. The catalog's deciding source (Hari, Taylor & Pike 1970, Part I sec. II.C, pp. 116-117: 'the basic word stress falls always on the first syllable of a word') was re-read and confirmed verbatim; no new source supersedes it. archive.org and ERIC were reached directly by URL.

new_statements.reading: Fixed initial word stress, weight-blind, independent of the four-way lexical tone (clear/breathy x level/falling); realized by onset intensity and slight length, not pitch. A phrase-final intonational prominence can overlay it but is explicitly attributed to higher-level intonation. This is the same passage the catalog already codes from; re-read in this search of works with stress in the title and confirmed verbatim (minor scanned errors 'matifested', 'onse' aside).

tone_statements.quote: Each monosyllabic word, in languages of the TGTM group, can carry one of four tones. The phonetic value (mainly pitch) of these tones varies from place to place ... the languages of the TGTM group do not distinguish four tones on each syllable of a word (which would make 16 melodies for a two-syllable word) but only four tones per word. ... In five dialects out of eight, Risiangku and Sahu Tamang, Tukche and Syang Thakali, and Ghachok Gurung, tone-1 and tone-2 words ‘are high with a clear voice quality; tone-3 and tone-4 are low with a breathy voice quality.

tone_statements.quote: Tamang has four tones - numbered 1 to 4, roughly from highest to lowest - which are phonetically complex. To the unaided ear of the linguist, these four tonal categories are distinguished by a combination of cues involving pitch level, pitch contour, and phonation type. [...] the domain of tone is the phonological word, composed of a lexical morpheme, which is tonally specified, and a sequence of tonally neutral suffixes. A single tonal melody spreads over the whole word. [...] Tone 1 is the highest; it tends to be shorter, and is falling; it gives the perceptual impression of a short, "ballistic" tone. Tone 2 lacks any salient characteristic apart from being the second highest; it is not whispery. Voicing of the initial stop, when present, identifies with certainty a tone as being either 3 or 4. Tone 3 is whispery and rising, within an overall low register. Tone 4 is low, somewhat whispery, and its falling contour is somewhat "ballistic", though less so than tone 1.

sources.quote: 'Tamang syllables appear to be all about equally stressed.' ... 'The languages of the Bodish section ... are poor in accentual contrasts. They do not generally give prominence, either by way of F0 or intensity, to one syllable per unit. Either all syllables have roughly equal prominence, as in the TGTM group, or one syllable per unit is weak.' (Her fieldwork is Risiangku = Eastern Tamang; statement is made for the Tamang/TGTM group. Same paper p.3 cites Hari, Taylor & Pike 1970:82 approvingly on the morpheme as tone domain.)
sources.note: Leading Tamang phonologist states TGTM/Tamang syllables have roughly equal prominence (no one-syllable stress) - a group-level counter-statement to fixed: initial syllable; should be cited as a caution on the record (Eastern-dialect based).

sources.quote: In the summer of 1969, Kenneth Pike, Austin Hale, and Doreen Taylor, working on Tamang with Karna Bahadur Tamang, came up with a three-tone, two-stress system with four classes ... a comparison of the many cognates which they share revealed that words which are (a) high stressed in Tamang are clear intense in Gurung and clear high level in Thakali, (b) unstressed in Tamang are clear relaxed in Gurung and clear extra-high falling in Thakali, (c) mid stressed in Tamang are breathy rising in Gurung and breathy low rising-falling in Thakali, and (d) low stressed in Tamang are breathy low in Gurung and breathy low level in Thakali

The phonetic value (mainly pitch) of these tones varies from place to place ... the languages of the TGTM group do not distinguish four tones on each syllable of a word (which would make 16 melodies for a two-syllable word) but only four tones per word. ... In five dialects out of eight, Risiangku and Sahu Tamang, Tukche and Syang Thakali, and Ghachok Gurung, tone-1 and tone-2 words ‘are high with a clear voice quality; tone-3 and tone-4 are low with a breathy voice quality.

sources.quote: Kenneth Pike, Austin Hale, and Doreen Taylor, working on Tamang with Karna Bahadur Tamang, Came up with a three-tone, two-stress system with four classes ... Stress, relative pitch, pitch contour, ... intensity and breathiness carry a high proportion of the functional load of the register system in T, Gu, and Th. ... Tamang word-bases may be (a) stressed with high pitch, (b) stressed with intermediate (mid) pitch, (c) stressed with low pitch, or (dad) unstressed.

sources.quote: The pairs above show us that there is not only a contrast between tense and lax voice quality, but within each group we have also a pitch contrast. In tense we have a high falling contour contrasting with a mid rising contour. The latter one is only slightly rising and in the contrast system it can be viewed as basically level. In lax a mid falling contour contrasts with a low slightly falling contour. In the description, the latter one is viewed as basically level. We have two contrast systems intersecting with each other: The voice quality contrast between lax and tense intersects with the pitch contrast between contour and basically level. This results in four different tone patterns.

sources.note: Bears on the tone half of the catalog class 'tone-and-stress' and is SILENT on word stress: the only 'stress' in the text is 'intonational stress' listed among phrase-final intonational features ('the end of a phonological phrase is signalled by various intonational features such as intonational stress, pitch rise, and upstep in pitch on the last syllable before the juncture', p. 27). Tone system as stated: four tone patterns = voice quality (tense vs lax; 'Tense articulation conditions high pitch', p. 2) x pitch (contour vs basically level): I tense high falling, II tense mid slightly-rising

sources.note: From the Crossref abstract: the TGTM tonal split (merger of onset voicing series > split of an old two-tone system into four) is phonologically completed in all dialects studied, but traces of manner and phonation (breathiness, residual onset voicing) survive to different degrees per dialect; proposes a 'law' that breathiness used as a tone cue is retained only while the tone's pitch stays low; dialect-by-dialect pitch values and cue retention for the four tones, Western Tamang (Sahugaon) among them.
